blocks.text: We have discussed the most commonly used Cartesian coordinate system. In effect, a frame of reference is any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken. For example, the position of a table in a room can be described relative to the walls of the room, making the room the frame of reference. Similarly, the laboratory is the frame of reference for measurements taken there; if the same experiment is performed in a moving train, the train becomes the frame of reference. The position of a spaceship can be described relative to the positions of distant stars, making a coordinate system based on these stars the frame of reference.
Inertial and non-inertial frames of reference

blocks.title: Inertial frame of reference
blocks.text: An inertial frame of reference is a coordinate system in which the law of inertia is valid: a body at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced force that produces acceleration. Other laws of nature also apply in such a system.

A body placed on the Earth remains at rest unless an unbalanced force acts upon it, indicating that the Earth can be considered an inertial frame of reference. A body in a car moving with uniform velocity relative to the Earth also remains at rest, so the car is also an inertial frame. Thus any frame of reference moving with uniform velocity relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame.

blocks.title: Non-inertial frame of reference
blocks.text: If the moving car is suddenly stopped or accelerated, the body inside no longer remains at rest; the car is then not an inertial frame. An accelerated frame of reference is a non-inertial frame.

While the Earth is rotating and revolving, which strictly makes it a non-inertial frame, it is often treated as an inertial frame because of its relatively small acceleration. Relativity is the study of the way in which observers in moving frames of reference perceive the world (For Your Information).
